d.title: A return type that varies with the path is the signal
d.caption: **Every Python function returns something — one with no `return`, or one that falls off the end, returns `None`.** The problem is not `None` itself; **it is a function whose return *type* varies with the path taken**, because every caller then needs a different set of checks and no two callers agree on which. The split follows the seams: **the decision that drives everything is routine versus exceptional — an empty id and a missing record mean the caller's assumption was wrong, so those raise; a record with no lines is a perfectly normal state, so that returns.**

d.title: How much docstring, decided by who reads it
d.caption: **A docstring that restates the signature earns nothing — the signature is already there, and type hints say the types.** So the amount is a function of the audience: **a short private helper needs a one-line summary or nothing at all if the name and hints say it; a public API needs Summary, Args, Returns and Raises, because callers cannot read your source.** And the two rows that always need text regardless of size: **a non-obvious constraint — idempotency, thread-safety, ordering, units — and anything surprising, where you document *why* rather than *what*.**

d.title: A slash buys back the freedom to rename a parameter
d.caption: **Without `/`, a parameter name is part of your public API forever — if nobody can write `x=3`, you can rename `x` to `dx` in a patch release.** That is the main reason, and two others follow. **Some names add nothing: `len(obj=[1,2,3])` is a `TypeError`, and rightly — `obj` carries no information a reader needed**, which is why many built-ins are positional-only. And **a function taking `**kwargs` cannot also accept a keyword matching one of its own parameters; making them positional-only removes the clash entirely** — which is what lets the output pass a `name` key straight through.

d.title: The same call twice, and the second one is missing a field
d.caption: **`*args` collects extra positionals into a tuple and `**kwargs` collects extra keywords into a dict** — so a logging wrapper can accept anything and pass it on. The output is the argument for being explicit about what you forward: **the first call carries `request_id` and `latency`, the second carries only `request_id`**, and nothing in the signature said either was expected. Which is the trade: **`**kwargs` makes a function accept everything, including a typo, so a misspelled keyword is silently collected rather than rejected.**

d.title: Three levels of default, and `None` stops working at the third
d.caption: The rules are short: **never a mutable literal (1.4), evaluate once at `def` time, and prefer `None` as the sentinel.** The third level is where people get stuck: **`None` works until `None` is itself a valid value the caller might pass — then you need a private sentinel object, which cannot be confused with anything a caller could supply.** The usual shape is a module-level `_MISSING = object()`, **and it is the only way to tell “argument omitted” from “argument explicitly `None`”.**

d.title: You need these only to assign, never to read
d.caption: **Reading follows LEGB automatically — `global` and `nonlocal` exist only so that an *assignment* writes somewhere other than the local scope.** The difference between them is where: **`global` writes to the module namespace, skipping enclosing scopes entirely; `nonlocal` writes to the nearest enclosing function's local.** And the asymmetry worth remembering: **`nonlocal` cannot create a name — it must already exist in an enclosing function — while `global` can create a module-level name that was never there.**

d.title: Four scope results, and only one of them matches the intuition from other languages
d.caption: **Python scopes at function level, not block level — so a name assigned inside an `if` or a `for` is visible after it, and a loop variable outlives the loop.** Which is why the second row prints at all. Then the two that look inconsistent and are not: **a comprehension has its own scope so the outer name is `unchanged` (2.11), and a class body is a scope that methods do not nest inside** — so a method cannot see a class-level name without going through `self` or the class.

d.title: partial freezes arguments and keeps the function inspectable
d.caption: **`partial(send, channel="ops", urgent=True)` returns a callable with those arguments already bound** — so the call site passes only what varies. The advantage over a lambda is the last row: **a `partial` object exposes `.func` and `.keywords`, so it prints as `send {'channel': 'ops', 'urgent': True}` and a debugger can tell you what it was built from.** A lambda closing over the same values shows you nothing. **Which is also why `partial` pickles and a lambda does not** — the difference that matters for multiprocessing.

d.title: The interface is the call signature
d.caption: **In languages without first-class functions, varying one behaviour means defining an interface and a class per implementation. In Python the interface *is* the call signature and each implementation is a function.** So the Strategy pattern collapses to a dict of functions and a lookup — 2.6's third dispatch shape — and the measured output is a discount of **80.00** selected by name. The limit is worth knowing: **once a strategy needs state, configuration or several related methods, a class earns its place back.**

d.title: Three cases, and the middle one is the one a comprehension cannot do cleanly
d.caption: A comprehension is the default and **`map` wins in exactly three situations.** The first is cosmetic — **`map(str.strip, lines)` beats `[s.strip() for s in lines]` when the function already exists, because the loop variable adds nothing.** The second is the real one: **`map(f, a, b)` iterates several sequences in parallel and stops at the shortest, which a comprehension needs `zip` to express.** And the third is laziness over a large or infinite source, **where `map` returns an iterator rather than building a list.**

d.title: Four results, and three of them have a built-in that says it better
d.caption: `reduce` folds a binary function over a sequence, and the measured values make the case against it: **24 is `math.prod`, 10 is `sum`, 4 is `max`** — all three read better as the named built-in, and `reduce` requires the reader to decode the lambda to find out which operation it was. **So what is left for `reduce` is the fourth row: a genuinely custom combine with no built-in equivalent** — merging configuration dicts left to right, composing functions, intersecting a list of sets. **And it moved out of builtins into `functools` in Python 3, which was a judgement about how often it is the right tool.**

d.title: Without wraps the function's identity is the wrapper's
d.caption: **A decorator returns a different function object, so unless you copy the metadata across, the decorated function reports the wrapper's name, no docstring and a signature of `(*args, **kwargs)`.** Which is not cosmetic: **`help()` shows the wrapper, a traceback names the wrapper, and introspection-driven tools — pytest fixtures, FastAPI route signatures, `inspect.signature` — read the wrong thing.** `functools.wraps` is one decorator on the inner function and it fixes all three, **and it also sets `__wrapped__` so the original is still reachable.**

d.title: `@expr` calls expr with the function, so a call needs one more layer
d.caption: **The reason is mechanical: `@expr` calls `expr` with the function. If `expr` is itself a call, its *result* must be the thing that takes the function** — hence three nested definitions rather than two. Read the equivalence: **`retry(times=5)` runs first and returns `decorator`; that result is then applied to `fetch`.** And the failure mode is specific: **forget the parentheses and the function itself becomes the `times` argument, so the error appears at the call site rather than at the decoration**, which is what makes it puzzling.

d.title: The question is whether the data is recursive, not whether the problem is
d.caption: **The first row decides most cases: trees, nested JSON, filesystems and expression grammars are recursive *data*, and a recursive traversal of recursive data is the clearest code there is.** The rest is about risk. **Depth that is bounded and known small — a JSON document, a parse tree — is safe; depth that is unbounded or user-controlled is a stack overflow waiting for the right input.** And the last row is the asymmetry: **iteration handles arbitrarily large input, which recursion cannot, whatever its depth limit is set to.**

d.title: Six renames, and each one answers a question the caller was going to ask
d.caption: The pattern is that **a verb says what happens and a noun says to what** — so `process(data)` tells a reader nothing and `normalise_addresses(addresses)` needs no docstring. Three carry real information beyond clarity: **`get` hides whether it hits the network, where `fetch` implies I/O and `find` implies it may return nothing; `is_` returns a bool where `validate` raises, and `check` could be either; and units belong in the name or the type, never in the docstring alone** — which is why `timeout_seconds=30` beats `timeout=30`.

d.title: `filters or {}` and `filters is None` differ, and the difference is a falsy value
d.caption: **For a dict the two are usually equivalent in effect — and they diverge the moment a falsy value is meaningful: `page or 1` silently rejects `page=0`, and `retries or 3` rejects `retries=0`** (1.7). There is a second, quieter reason to prefer the explicit test: **`filters or {}` also creates a new dict when an *empty* one is passed, silently discarding the caller's object** — harmless for a filter and surprising for anything the caller intended to keep a reference to.
